terrainNotes: Elevation data at this point, finest first: LOLA LDEM_80S_20M, 60 m site window (60 m per sample, to about 3.8 km); LOLA south pole, 85S square at 80 m (80 m per sample, to about 14 km); LOLA south pole, 80S square at 160 m (160 m per sample, to about 166 km); LOLA LDEM_80S_20M, 480 m site window (480 m per sample, to about 31 km); LOLA whole-Moon grid, 16 px/deg (1.9 km per sample, whole Moon).
Beyond about 166 km from the site only the whole-Moon grid is available (1.9 km per sample), which smooths ridges narrower than that; distant skyline peaks can read slightly low.

Where one grid hands over to the next, the heights do not match exactly. Around this site the outer grid differs from the inner one by: -2.9 to +4.1 m (0.7 m RMS) at 3.8 km, where the 60 m window ends. A skyline point formed right at such an edge is uncertain by about that much: 1 m of height is 0.015° at 3.8 km.
assumptions: Observer 2 m above the terrain at -84.7900, 29.2000 (degrees, east-positive, ME frame); heights above the 1737.4 km sphere.
Positions are topocentric and airless (no refraction), as JPL Horizons APPARENT=AIRLESS for a coord@301 observer.

Skyline from elevation data, including the Moon's curvature, 0.5 deg in azimuth, searched to 188 km: LOLA LDEM_80S_20M, 60 m site window (60 m) from 0.0 to 5.4 km; LOLA south pole, 85S square at 80 m (80 m) from 3.9 to 130.7 km; LOLA south pole, 80S square at 160 m (160 m) from 13.6 to 175.9 km; LOLA whole-Moon grid, 16 px/deg (1895 m) from 165.2 to 188.5 km.
Sampled every 10 min; rise and set times refined to 10 s; the Sun and Earth are discs (visible fraction integrated across each disc).

A rise or set takes time, so each event is one named instant (decision D-8): sunrise = the first part of the Sun's disc appears above the skyline ("Sun starts rising"), sunset = the last part goes behind it ("Sun fully set"); Earthrise / Earthset = Earth's centre crossing the skyline. Each event's span (and `transitions`) gives the whole passage: from the first cut of the disc to the last limb when setting, from the first limb to the whole disc clear when rising.
Sunlight also counts Earth passing in front of the Sun (geometric discs; the faint light refracted by Earth's atmosphere is ignored).

Earth visibility is geometric line of sight only; it says nothing about a working radio link. "Earth in view" (earthVisiblePct) counts Earth's centre above the skyline; earthAnyPct counts any part of Earth's disc, the definition of the PGDA long-term Earth map.
Slope over a 120 m baseline from LOLA LDEM_80S_20M, 60 m site window, 60 m: hazards smaller than the grid are not seen.

warnings: Beyond about 166 km from the site only the whole-Moon grid is available (1.9 km per sample), which smooths ridges narrower than that; distant skyline peaks can read slightly low.

The longest darkness runs into the edge of the window: it is a lower bound.
The longest Earth gap runs into the edge of the window: it is a lower bound.
The longest darkness that touches this window lasts 350.0 h in full, from 2026-12-30 08:00 to 2027-01-13 22:00 UTC; the window itself holds 310.0 h of it at most in one stretch.

The longest spell without Earth's centre in view that touches this window lasts 133.1 h in full, from 2026-12-31 07:52 to 2027-01-05 20:58 UTC; the window itself holds 117.0 h of it at most in one stretch.

station.name: Madrid DSS-63 (70 m)
station.complex: Robledo de Chavela, near Madrid, Spain

assumptions: Geometry only: an opportunity is an unobstructed straight line between the station and the site, with the site above the station's elevation limit and the station above the site's terrain skyline. It is not a statement about a working radio link: no link budget, frequency, antenna pattern, antenna scheduling or availability is considered.

Stations: the 70 m antennas DSS-14 (Goldstone), DSS-43 (Canberra) and DSS-63 (Madrid). Coordinates from the DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook, 810-005, Module 301 Rev. N (15 April 2022), Tables 2 and 5 (ITRF93 epoch 2003.0; WGS 84).

Elevation limits: 6.0 deg for receiving (the handbook's generic receive limit; the antennas' mechanical limit is about 6 deg) and, for transmitting, 10.4 deg at DSS-14 and 10.2 deg at DSS-43 and DSS-63 (the limits of the handbook's 70 m transmit coverage chart). The stations' own azimuth-dependent horizon masks are not applied: for instance the handbook keeps DSS-63 above 20.2 deg towards high ground to its north-west when transmitting, and high-power transmitters have higher limits.
At the site the direction to the station itself is tested against the skyline (the stations are up to 0.95 deg from the centre of Earth's disc).

Positions are geometric and airless (no tropospheric refraction); Earth's rotation uses UT1 = UTC without polar motion. Checked against JPL Horizons, the site as seen from each station: elevation within 0.0013 deg over 1154 instants (1971, 2025, 2034) and rise and set times through the limits within 0.3 s on the day compared; UT1 - UTC, at most 0.9 s, is the limit in general.

highlights: Sunlight per lunar day ranges from 35.5 % (lunar day 5, from 2027-04-29) to 52.2 % (lunar day 11, from 2027-10-23) over the 12 from 2027-01-01.
Earth's centre is in view from 73.2 % (lunar day 1) to 84.7 % (lunar day 11) of a lunar day (geometric line of sight).
The longest darkness in the span lasts 411.7 h (17.2 days), from 2027-04-25 19:17 to 2027-05-12 22:58 UTC.

For a 14-day mission, arriving 2027-10-06 12:00 UTC scores highest in this span, 100.0 (100.0 % sunlight, 100.0 % Earth line of sight, longest darkness 0.0 h); arriving 2027-12-19 14:00 UTC scores lowest, 31.8 (0.0 % sunlight, 63.6 % Earth line of sight, longest darkness 336.0 h). The planned arrival, 2027-01-01 00:00 UTC, scores 36.2 (7.1 % sunlight, 65.2 % Earth line of sight, longest darkness 310.0 h).
A slip of 7 days from the planned arrival changes sunlight from 7.1 % to 57.1 %, Earth line of sight from 65.2 % to 100.0 % and the longest darkness from 310.0 h to 142.0 h.
assumptions: Span: 12 lunar months of 29.530589 days from 2027-01-01 00:00 UTC; rows are consecutive lunar days from that instant.

Observer 2 m above the terrain at -84.7900, 29.2000 (degrees, east-positive). One skyline for the whole span, 0.5 deg in azimuth, from: LOLA LDEM_80S_20M, 60 m site window (60 m) from 0.0 to 5.4 km; LOLA south pole, 85S square at 80 m (80 m) from 3.9 to 130.7 km; LOLA south pole, 80S square at 160 m (160 m) from 13.6 to 175.9 km; LOLA whole-Moon grid, 16 px/deg (1895 m) from 165.2 to 188.5 km.

Sun and Earth from the in-app model for the whole span (In-app model (astronomy-engine + IAU lunar rotation, light-time and aberration applied, airless): within 0.004 deg of JPL Horizons topocentric airless az/el (DE441) in all validation samples 1969-2035. Directions computed every 3 h and interpolated (agreeing with the model to better than 0.0005 deg).), sampled every 20 min; rise and set times refined to 10 s. Topocentric and airless.

Sunlight is the time-averaged visible fraction of the Sun's disc; Earth passing in front of the Sun is included. Earth line of sight means Earth's centre above the skyline: geometry only, not a radio link. Each row's earthAnyPct counts any part of Earth's disc instead (the definition of PGDA product 69's long-term Earth map).
Darkness and Earth gaps are measured in full: they are not cut at a row's edges, and at the ends of the span they are followed up to 60 days further.
Arrivals: a mission of 336.0 h starting every 2.0 h across the span; score = weighted mean of sunlight % and Earth line-of-sight % (weights 1 and 1), the score of the nearby ranking.
These are geometric conditions only; nothing here is a statement about power or temperature.

Around this site the outer grid differs from the inner one by: -2.9 to +4.1 m (0.7 m RMS) at 3.8 km, where the 60 m window ends. A skyline point formed right at such an edge is uncertain by about that much: 1 m of height is 0.015° at 3.8 km.
